Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 2003 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they generally ignore whatever a company's management is saying, analyze the "fuzzy" importance of intrinsic value, and identify the one word that's a sure sign of earnings trouble. Buffett also recounts a funny anecdote about not letting an executive with second thoughts wriggle out of a deal.

Sat, May 3 2003 • 1:00 PM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 2. Read everything, ignore management, wait for "fat pitch"
  2. 5. "Intrinsic value is terribly important and very fuzzy"
  3. 14. Clayton Homes is "class player" in manufactured homes industry
  4. 17. Munger on recognizing "bullshit earnings"
  5. 24. Buffett: I don't ask my friends for favors
  6. 27. Simple compensation plans and no consultants
1. Pretax operating profits clarification

6. Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae, and systemic derivatives risk

WARREN BUFFETT: Number 4.

Sync Video to Paragraph

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Hi. I'm John Golob from Kansas City. I have a follow up question on derivatives.

Sync Video to Paragraph

After the press zeroed in on the comments in your annual letter, the head of Fannie Mae got up and said, well, Mr. Buffett's criticisms don't apply to Fannie because, number 1, we have simple vanilla derivatives that are priced in the market. And secondly, we need derivatives to protect against interest rate risk.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I guess, given what happened to the savings and loan industry back in the '80s, that seems reasonable.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So my first question is what is your rejoinder to Mr. Raines?

Sync Video to Paragraph

And the second part of my question gets to your concern about the connection between derivatives and systemic risk. And that is, do Fannie and Freddie play a particularly prominent role in this concern? Thank you.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. I have a lot of respect for Frank Raines. I think he's done a good job at Fannie Mae. I don't know the situation intimately.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The problem, as you mention, is that an operation like Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, or savings and loans in the past, had this problem, which is inherent in the mortgage instrument, in matching â or coming close to matching â assets and liabilities.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And the reason they had that terrible problem, which did in many institutions, was the optionality in a mortgage instrument.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And in a mortgage instrument, particularly as the years have progressed, you buy a â you know, if you buy a mortgage â or somebody else takes out the mortgage, you own it â you have a 30-year instrument if it's a bad deal and you have about a 30-minute instrument if it's a good deal.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The buyer â the person who takes out the mortgage â can call off the deal at any time at relatively low cost. And the public has been sensitized to that more and more as time has gone by, so they've been quicker to refinance for very small differentials.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, many years ago, they had what they called due-on-sale clauses in California. I think â were they invalidated, Charlie, or what happened with those? So that there were ways of shortening up the mortgage expected maturities.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But it's a fundamental problem when you are operating on borrowed money in a very big way, which is what S&Ls did and what Fannie does, and Freddie, that you have this very long-term instrument, and it â but it can be very short-term if it becomes advantageous to you, and rates go down and you want to keep it. Or it becomes very long-term if rates go up and nobody wants to refinance.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And under those circumstances, if you run a huge institution, or even a smaller one, but that has a high â highly leveraged, you are going to look for one way or another to try to match the duration of your liabilities as close as you can to the duration of your assets, and have various methods to protect yourself against the optionality that exists with the counterparty, in effect, your asset.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That's not easy to do. And Fannie, and Freddie, and other institutions, attempt to do that through various types of derivative instruments, as well as other things, in terms of the kind of debt they issue themselves and so on.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And they're very smart, and they do it â you know, my guess is they do a better job than Charlie and I could do at it, but it can't, by its nature, be perfect.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And under some circumstances, where you get large gaps â the thing you worry about in financial markets, and it doesn't happen very often, but your â the thing that really destroys people are what the academics would call six-sigma, or five-sigma, or seven-sigma events, which are things that are never supposed to happen, basically.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And sigma is a method of describing the probabilities that they will happen in any given period â the number of sigmas.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Financial markets don't lend themselves well to modeling based on that. You know, they do most of the time, until it doesn't work. And when it doesn't work, you know, chaos reigns.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And there are more six-sigma events that happen in financial markets â or theoretical six- sigma events â than any study of probability curves would ever come up with.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And thatâs â when you have gaps or discontinuities, when markets close, whatever it may be, those are what cause institutions to go out of business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And derivatives, in my view, anyway, accentuate the possibility of it happening and the extent of the damage, if and when it should happen.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Again, we don't think we mathematically can tell you what the probabilities are of something like that, and we think anybody that does tell you, you know, is kidding you.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I've had managers of hedge funds sit down with me and tell me that they had, you know, a 28 percent probability of returns between 30 and 40 percent. Come up with all these exact figures. Anybody comes up with exact figures in finance, watch out.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, I would say that if I were running Fannie or Freddie, I would be terribly conscious of what was happening in there, and I would understand this basic problem I have, which I can guarantee you, Frank Raines understands extremely well, of the optionality built into his assets.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I would try to come as close to matching that. And if I did it through derivative instruments or whatever, I would try to match â I would try to reduce the troubles that could be produced by that optionality to a minimum.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And then I would get very worried about who the counterparties were, because anytime somebody promises to pay you a lot of money if something terrible happens to you, you better be very sure that they can and will pay, because the terrible thing that's happening to you may be presenting terrible things to them.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You know, that will happen in the insurance industry from time to time. And that's why reinsurance recoverables are a dangerous asset to have.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It will happen in the derivative markets.

Sync Video to Paragraph

When LTCM had troubles with one type of asset, they had troubles with a lot of types of assets, and everybody else they were doing business with was having a lot of troubles with those same things.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that's why the Federal Reserve stepped into something they never dreamt they would have stepped into. They stepped in to force, essentially, a solution, which may have been the right thing to do, incidentally.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But they â for some obscure hedge fund that nobody in the world virtually had heard of, until that point, and had started threatening the U.S. â the stability of the U.S. financial system.
